Pottiaceae
A large moss family; many species tolerate exposed, seasonally dry ground.
Moss family Pottiaceae.
Buxbaumiaceae
Mosses with greatly reduced leafy gametophytes and conspicuous sporophyte capsules.
Buxbaumia moss family.
Malpighiaceae
A mostly tropical family of trees, shrubs and lianas; many have opposite leaves and winged fruits.
Malpighia family.
Bladderwort family
Carnivorous herbs including bladderworts, whose tiny suction traps capture small aquatic or soil organisms.
Bladderwort family.
Blunt-leaved acaulon moss
Acaulon muticum
Acaulon moss.

A minute annual moss of open, often disturbed bare soil. The leafy shoots are only a few millimetres tall; a few concave upper leaves partly surround the nearly sessile, globose capsule. The capsule and its very short seta are the most conspicuous field characters. The plate greatly enlarges this tiny plant for visibility.
Scattered in temperate Europe and elsewhere; grows on exposed, often calcareous soil. Local occurrence varies and the moss is easily overlooked.
Tiny cushion-like shoot with a terminal capsule on a very short seta.
Few small concave leaves clustered around the capsule, with blunt to shortly pointed tips.
Mosses do not form flowers; the enlarged study shows the upper leafy shoot.
Spherical moss capsule containing spores, held close to the shoot.
White quebracho
Aspidosperma quebracho-blanco
Quebracho blanco; white quebracho.

A long-lived dry-forest tree with a rounded crown, pale deeply fissured bark and small, leathery, simple leaves. Its small pale flowers are followed by paired woody follicles that open to release flat, papery-winged seeds. The very hard wood is a notable feature; traditional uses are not evidence of safe medicinal use.
Gran Chaco and adjacent dry regions of Argentina, Bolivia, Paraguay and Uruguay.
Medium-sized evergreen to briefly deciduous tree with a broad crown and rugged trunk.
Small, simple, leathery leaf with an entire margin.
Small pale flowers borne in short clusters.
Paired rounded follicles open to expose flat, membranous-winged seeds.
Caapi vine
Banisteriopsis caapi
Ayahuasca vine; caapi.

A woody tropical liana with opposite, entire leaves and small pinkish flowers. Its dry fruit is a three-winged samara, a useful Malpighiaceae character. The species has important Indigenous cultural contexts and contains potent psychoactive compounds; this botanical profile is descriptive and makes no preparation or use recommendation.
Native to tropical South America, especially humid Amazonian forests; cultivated and transported beyond its native range.
Woody climbing vine using surrounding trees for support.
Opposite simple leaf, broadly oval, with an entire edge and a pointed tip.
Small pink to rose flowers in axillary or terminal clusters.
Dry samara with three prominent wings; the third wing can be partly hidden in a side view.
Lava cactus
Brachycereus nesioticus
Galápagos lava cactus.

A columnar, clump-forming cactus that pioneers bare Galápagos lava. Pale young spines can make stems look silvery; age darkens the stems. Large yellow flowers open near the stem tips and are followed by fleshy reddish fruits. It is a Galápagos endemic adapted to harsh, exposed volcanic ground.
Endemic to the Galápagos Islands, growing on young lava flows and rocky coastal sites.
Cluster of erect, ribbed cylindrical stems, often pale from dense spines.
Cacti lack ordinary leaves; the green ribbed stem performs photosynthesis and bears areoles with spines.
Large yellow flower arising from an areole near a stem tip.
Fleshy reddish fruit developing from the flower; the illustrated fruit color varies with maturity.
Green shield-moss
Buxbaumia viridis
Green bug-on-a-stick moss.

An unusual moss whose leafy gametophyte is extremely reduced and difficult to see. Its conspicuous sporophyte has a long seta and an oblong green capsule with a sloping, asymmetric profile. It typically grows on decaying conifer wood in cool, humid, shaded forests; suitable deadwood and stable moisture are important habitat conditions.
Scattered through cool, humid parts of Europe and other northern regions; localized on decaying wood in shaded forests.
One or a few prominent sporophytes rising from a nearly invisible leafy phase on rotten wood.
Gametophyte leaves are minute and rarely visible; the capsule is the practical recognition feature.
Mosses have no flowers; the separate close-up shows the sporophyte stalk and capsule.
Oblong, asymmetric spore capsule on a seta; technically a capsule, not a fruit.
Rough coddia
Coddia rudis
Rough-leaved coddia.

A rigid southern African shrub with small obovate leaves often clustered on short shoots. Its solitary white to yellowish flowers have the fused corolla typical of Rubiaceae. A rounded fruit with a persistent calyx crown follows flowering. The combination of leaf clusters and calyx-crowned fruit helps distinguish it from superficially similar dryland shrubs.
Southern Africa, especially dry scrub and rocky habitats in South Africa and neighboring regions.
Compact, intricately branched shrub with short rigid branchlets.
Small obovate leaves clustered on short shoots, with a blunt or rounded tip.
Solitary small white to cream flower with a tubular, four-lobed corolla.
Rounded fruit topped by the persistent calyx lobes.
Chilean lantern tree
Crinodendron hookerianum
Chilean lantern tree; chaquihue.

An evergreen Chilean shrub or small tree with alternate, narrow, finely toothed leaves. Its distinctive red flowers hang singly on long stalks and form an inflated lantern-like, five-part structure. The dry fruit is a three-valved capsule. It belongs to humid temperate forests and is not a native European species.
Endemic to southern Chile, in humid temperate forest and forest margins.
Evergreen shrub or small tree with slender branches and pendent flowers.
Alternate lanceolate leaf with a pointed tip and fine serrations.
Pendent red lantern-like flower with five fused or closely joined petals.
Dry capsule with three valves; shown separately from the flowering plant.
Ackermann’s disocactus
Disocactus ackermannii
Ackermann’s epiphyllum.

An epiphytic forest cactus with flattened, jointed photosynthetic stems, not true leaves. The older basal stems become more woody while the flat upper segments have scalloped margins and small areoles. Large scarlet flowers emerge from the areoles; a small fleshy fruit may follow. The plate shows the accepted name Disocactus ackermannii.
Native to humid forests of southern Mexico; grows on trees or rocks rather than as a desert ground cactus.
Arching epiphytic cactus with flat segmented cladodes and showy red flowers.
The apparent leaf is a flattened photosynthetic stem segment with small marginal areoles.
Large scarlet funnel-shaped flower with numerous narrow perianth segments.
Small fleshy berry developing from the flower; fruit is less often seen in cultivation.
Asam kelubi palm
Eleiodoxa conferta
Asam kelubi; nipa swamp palm.

A clustering swamp palm with an underground stem, long pinnate leaves and spiny leaf stalks. Its inflorescences arise at ground level, and the scaly reddish-brown fruits are borne in dense clusters. The tart fruit is traditionally eaten or fermented in parts of Southeast Asia; edible use varies by preparation and does not imply that unidentified palm fruits are safe.
Lowland peat and freshwater swamps of the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra and Borneo.
Clump-forming palm with subterranean stems and arching pinnate fronds.
Long pinnate frond with narrow leaflets and spines along the petiole or rachis.
Inflorescence emerging close to ground level from the base of the palm.
Dense cluster of pear-shaped, reddish-brown, scaly drupes.
Chiotilla cactus
Escontria chiotilla
Quiotilla; chiotilla.

A tree-like, much-branched columnar cactus of seasonally dry southern Mexico. Its ribbed green stems carry areoles with spines; small yellow flowers arise near stem tips, followed by scaly purple-red fruits. The fruit is locally harvested and sold, but the species identification should be confirmed before any food use.
Endemic to dry tropical regions of southern Mexico, including Oaxaca and Puebla.
Arborescent cactus with a short trunk and many ascending ribbed branches.
No ordinary leaves; spines arise from areoles on the photosynthetic ribbed stem.
Small yellow flower borne near the end of a mature stem.
Fleshy purple-red fruit with a scaly outer surface.
Sandy everlasting
Helichrysum arenarium
Dwarf everlast; sandy everlasting.

A low perennial of dry, sandy ground, covered in a dense grey-white woolly indumentum. Short shoots bear narrow leaves and compact clusters of golden flower heads with dry papery involucral bracts. The fruits are small achenes with a pappus. Medicinal traditions exist, but efficacy and safety are outside this identification profile.
Central and eastern Europe eastward into temperate Asia, on dry sandy grassland and open woodland.
Low, woolly perennial with short upright flowering stems and clustered golden heads.
Narrow alternate leaves covered on both surfaces by pale woolly hairs.
Dense golden head of tiny florets surrounded by papery yellow bracts.
Small dry achene with a tuft of bristles (pappus) for dispersal.
Common sea-lavender
Limonium vulgare
Common sea-lavender; sea lavender.

A salt-marsh perennial with a basal rosette of leathery leaves and branched, angular flowering stems. Its small flowers are grouped in compact spikelets; the persistent coloured calyx remains conspicuous after the petals fade. Taxonomy in Limonium is complex and hybridization occurs, so exact field identification may require a regional key.
Coastal salt marshes of western Europe, especially Atlantic and North Sea shores.
Basal rosette sending up several branched sprays of small flowers.
Leathery basal leaf, usually oblong to lanceolate, with a narrowed base.
Compact spikelets with minute flowers and a persistent purple calyx.
Small one-seeded utricle enclosed by the persistent calyx.
Heller’s prickly pear
Opuntia galapageia var. helleri
Opuntia helleri (tree name; synonym); Heller’s prickly pear.

A Galápagos prickly pear with jointed, flattened cladodes and areoles bearing spines or glochids. Yellow flowers develop into fleshy fruits. POWO accepts this taxon as Opuntia galapageia var. helleri and lists Opuntia helleri as a synonym; the living-tree name is preserved and matched through that explicit synonym.
Endemic to several northern Galápagos islands, including Darwin, Genovesa, Marchena and Wolf.
Succulent branching cactus with an upright trunk and flattened pads.
The visible pads are flattened stems (cladodes); minute leaves are transient, while areoles bear glochids and spines.
Yellow many-parted flower arising from an areole near a pad margin.
Fleshy reddish to purplish fruit with areoles and glochids on its surface.
Baron’s pachypodium
Pachypodium baronii
Baron’s pachypodium; red-flowered pachypodium.

A succulent Madagascan shrub with a markedly swollen bottle-shaped base, spiny branches and terminal clusters of broad leaves. Its large crimson flowers distinguish it from several close congeners. The related Windsor form has sometimes been treated as a variety or species; this profile follows POWO’s species-level concept and excludes varietal claims not needed for identification.
Endemic to northern Madagascar, on rocky slopes and exposed outcrops; threatened by habitat loss and collection.
Succulent shrub with an inflated caudex-like base, sparse spiny branches and terminal leaf rosettes.
Broad obovate leaves clustered near branch tips, with a visible midrib.
Large crimson-red funnel flower, often with a pale throat.
Paired narrow follicles release seeds with a tuft of hairs; fruit is shown separately from the flowering whole plant.
Banana passionfruit
Passiflora tarminiana
Banana passionfruit; curuba (regional name).

A vigorous climbing passionflower with three-lobed, toothed leaves and solitary flowers on long stalks. The flower has a long green floral tube, pale pink reflexed petals and a purple-and-pink outer corona; the elongated berry ripens yellow to orange. It is distinct from the often-confused Passiflora tripartita var. mollissima. The fruit is used as food in its range; the vine is invasive where introduced in some regions.
Native from southern Mexico through Central America and the tropical Andes; cultivated and naturalized elsewhere.
High-climbing tendril-bearing vine with pubescent stems.
Three-lobed leaf with coarse teeth and small glands on the petiole.
Long tubular flower with three bracts, reflexed pink petals and a purple spotted corona.
Elongated yellow-orange berry with orange pulp and numerous seeds.
Pistachio
Pistacia vera
Pistachio tree; pistachio.

A deciduous, drought-adapted tree with pinnate leaves and separate male and female individuals. Small apetalous flowers are borne in panicles. The commercial pistachio is botanically a drupe: its fleshy outer layers surround a hard shell and the edible seed inside. Orchards need pollen from male trees for female trees to set a crop.
Native from northeastern Iran and Central Asia into Afghanistan; widely cultivated in dry regions.
Small to medium deciduous tree with a broad, irregular crown.
Alternate pinnate leaf, commonly with three to five broad oval leaflets.
Small greenish flowers in branched panicles; male and female flowers occur on separate trees.
Clustered drupes; the edible portion is the seed inside the split hard endocarp, not the fleshy outer layer.
Garden rhubarb
Rheum rhabarbarum
Rhubarb; garden rhubarb.

A large perennial with broad basal leaves on thick, often reddish petioles and a tall branched flower panicle. Its fruit is a three-winged achene. Rhubarb cultivars have complex horticultural histories; the leaf stalk is the part conventionally cooked as food, while the leaf blades are not eaten because of their oxalate content.
Native range reported from southern Siberia to northern and central China; widely cultivated in temperate gardens.
Clump-forming perennial with a short rhizome, massive basal leaves and a tall flowering stem.
Large cordate to rounded blade with a wavy margin and a long, thick petiole.
Small greenish flowers in a tall, much-branched panicle.
Small dry achene with three conspicuous wings.
Common glasswort
Salicornia europaea
Common glasswort; marsh samphire.

A small annual halophyte with fleshy, jointed, freely branched stems and opposite scale-like leaves pressed against the stem, giving a leafless appearance. Tiny flowers are embedded in terminal fertile segments, usually in groups of three with the central flower larger. The Salicornia europaea group is taxonomically difficult and regional concepts differ; the plate illustrates the traditional species concept and cannot replace a local key. Do not use a visual match alone to decide that a wild plant is edible.
Coastal salt marshes and other saline habitats across much of Europe; local limits and separation from close taxa vary by flora.
Low, erect or semi-erect annual with succulent jointed stems and many branches.
Minute opposite scale leaves fused closely around each fleshy stem segment.
Tiny flowers embedded in fertile stem segments; central flower usually larger than the two lateral flowers.
Small one-seeded achene retained within a fleshy fertile segment.
Common rue
Ruta graveolens
Garden rue; rue.

An aromatic perennial subshrub with a woody base, blue-green leaves divided into rounded segments, and terminal clusters of yellow flowers. The central flower is usually five-parted, while lateral flowers commonly have four petals; the fruit is a lobed capsule. Contact with rue followed by sunlight can cause phototoxic skin inflammation, blistering and pigmentation. Avoid medicinal or culinary recommendations.
Native to the Mediterranean region and western Asia; cultivated and naturalized in many temperate regions.
Small branching subshrub with a woody base and blue-green aromatic foliage.
Alternate, finely divided leaf with rounded segments and visible oil glands.
Yellow terminal cluster; lateral flowers commonly have four petals, central flower five.
Green lobed capsule containing small dark seeds.
Humboldt’s bladderwort
Utricularia humboldtii
Humboldt bladderwort.

A large tropical bladderwort that may grow in water held by the central tanks of bromeliads on the Guiana Shield tepuis. Its simple leaves vary from wedge-shaped to broad and kidney-shaped. A slender scape bears purple flowers with a conspicuous yellow or orange palate and a long spur. Stolons carry tiny suction bladders that trap minute prey; these bladders are not pitchers and belong to the bladderwort itself.
Guiana Shield highlands, especially tepui habitats in Venezuela, Guyana and northern Brazil.
Rootless carnivorous herb with stolons, leaves and a separate upright flower stalk, sometimes in bromeliad tanks.
Simple floating or emergent blade, variable from obovate to broadly reniform.
Purple bilabiate corolla with a bright yellow to orange palate and a long narrow spur.
Small capsule; the diagnostic vegetative detail is an oval suction bladder on a stolon.
